title: Querying and Summarizing Census PUMS Data in R
text:
We will manipulate and process data sets from Public Use Microdata Sample (PUMS) census API. We are focusing on datasets for years 2021, 2022, 2023, and 2024.

# tidyverse attaches dplyr, tibble, purrr, ggplot2, and lubridate. httr makes the web requests and jsonlite parses JSON.
library(httr)
library(jsonlite)
library(tidyverse)

title: Querying and Summarizing Census PUMS Data in R
text:
Checking function on year 2024
Check the parser output. Input year 2024. The output should be 15 variables and SEX should show its two codes Male and Female.

vars_2024 <- get_pums_variables(2024)
names(vars_2024)

 [1] "AGEP"     "GASP"     "GRPIP"    "JWAP"     "JWDP"     "JWMNP"   
 [7] "PWGTP"    "FER"      "HHL"      "SCH"      "SCHL"     "SEX"     
[13] "REGION"   "DIVISION" "STATE"   

vars_2024$SEX$items

       1        2 
  "Male" "Female" 


The names are the 14 variables the project asks for plus STATE, and SEX has two codes: 1 is Male and 2 is Female.
The state variable is called ST in the 2021 and 2022 files. The parser should hide that difference, so asking for 2021 should still give a list that contains STATE.

vars_2021 <- get_pums_variables(2021)
"STATE" %in% names(vars_2021)

[1] TRUE


The year check should reject anything outside 2021 to 2024. The chunk below is set to keep rendering after an error so the message shows on the page.

get_pums_variables(2020)

Error in `get_pums_variables()`:
! year must be a single value: 2021, 2022, 2023, or 2024


The parser was shown to run successfully for 2024. Now we run it on all years and save the results for later code to reference.

title: Querying and Summarizing Census PUMS Data in R
section: Building the lists for all four years
text:
Building the lists for all four years
One list per year is built and saved to data/pums_variables.rds. The if statement prevents redownloading on rerenders.The saved lists are then read back in as pums_vars.

if (!file.exists("data/pums_variables.rds")) {
  pums_variable_lists <- lapply(2021:2024, get_pums_variables)
  names(pums_variable_lists) <- 2021:2024
  dir.create("data", showWarnings = FALSE)
  saveRDS(pums_variable_lists, "data/pums_variables.rds")
}

pums_vars <- readRDS("data/pums_variables.rds")

Check the lists. The list is indexed by year and each year holds the 15 variables.

names(pums_vars)

[1] "2021" "2022" "2023" "2024"

names(pums_vars[["2024"]])

 [1] "AGEP"     "GASP"     "GRPIP"    "JWAP"     "JWDP"     "JWMNP"   
 [7] "PWGTP"    "FER"      "HHL"      "SCH"      "SCHL"     "SEX"     
[13] "REGION"   "DIVISION" "STATE"   

pums_vars[["2024"]]$SEX$items

       1        2 
  "Male" "Female" 

length(pums_vars[["2021"]]$STATE$items)

[1] 52


The first two lines confirm the four years and the 15 variables per year. The third shows the mappings for SEX. The last shows that the state list has 52 entries, the 50 states, DC, and Puerto Rico. Puerto Rico will be dropped when state input is validated.

title: Querying and Summarizing Census PUMS Data in R
text:
Parsing an API response
A request to the PUMS API consists of the base address for the year, a get= list of variables, a for= clause for the geography, any optional filters, and the key. Before writing the main query function, one small request shows what the API sends back. This one asks for sex, person weight, age, arrival time at work, travel time to work, and education for people in North Carolina (for=state:37) who are 30 years old with a 45 minute commute (AGEP=30&JWMNP=45), which keeps the response short.
The key is read from the CENSUS_KEY environment variable instead of being typed into the document, because this code is published with the site.

census_key <- Sys.getenv("CENSUS_KEY")
stopifnot("Set CENSUS_KEY in .Renviron and restart R" = nzchar(census_key))
 
url <- paste0("https://api.census.gov/data/2024/acs/acs1/pums",
              "?get=SEX,PWGTP,AGEP,JWAP,JWMNP,SCHL",
              "&for=state:37&AGEP=30&JWMNP=45",
              "&key=", census_key)
resp <- GET(url)
status_code(resp)

[1] 200

cat(substr(content(resp, as = "text", encoding = "UTF-8"), 1, 300))

[["SEX","PWGTP","AGEP","JWAP","JWMNP","SCHL","AGEP","JWMNP","state"],
["1","76","30","88","45","22","30","45","37"],
["1","77","30","94","45","20","30","45","37"],
["1","279","30","103","45","21","30","45","37"],
["1","50","30","85","45","17","30","45","37"],
["1","12","30","79","45","16","30","45",


A status of 200 means the request was successful. In the JSON body returned, the first array is the header and each following array is one person’s record. Every value arrives as a string. AGEP and JWMNP appear twice. The API repeats any variable used as a filter at the end of each row. The geography comes back as a column named state.
The first helper turns the JSON text into a tibble. It uses the first row as the column names and drops any repeated column. First it checks if the return is JSON to ensure there is no error response.

# Turn the text of a Census API reply into a tibble of character columns.
# The reply is an array of arrays: row 1 is the header, the rest is data.
parse_census_json <- function(json_text) {
  if (!validate(json_text)) {
    stop("The Census API did not return JSON. The reply began: ",
         substr(json_text, 1, 200), call. = FALSE)
  }
  mat <- fromJSON(json_text)             # a character matrix
  colnames(mat) <- mat[1, ]
  # Variables used as filters are repeated at the end; keep the first copy
  mat <- mat[-1, !duplicated(colnames(mat)), drop = FALSE]
  as_tibble(mat)
}

The second helper works on the object GET() returns. It checks the HTTP status and stops with the API’s own message when something is wrong. For example, a misspelled variable name produces a status 400 with a short explanation, and a query that matches no records produces a 204. Otherwise it passes the text to the first helper.

# Convert the object returned by GET() into a tibble.
pums_response_to_tibble <- function(resp) {
  reply <- content(resp, as = "text", encoding = "UTF-8")
  if (status_code(resp) == 204) {
    stop("The query matched no records.", call. = FALSE)
  }
  if (status_code(resp) != 200) {
    stop("Census API request failed (status ", status_code(resp), "): ",
         reply, call. = FALSE)
  }
  parse_census_json(reply)
}

Applying it to the response from above gives a tibble with one row per person.

census_raw <- pums_response_to_tibble(resp)
census_raw

# A tibble: 58 × 7
   SEX   PWGTP AGEP  JWAP  JWMNP SCHL  state
   <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr> <chr>
 1 1     76    30    88    45    22    37   
 2 1     77    30    94    45    20    37   
 3 1     279   30    103   45    21    37   
 4 1     50    30    85    45    17    37   
 5 1     12    30    79    45    16    37   
 6 1     64    30    79    45    22    37   
 7 2     93    30    76    45    21    37   
 8 2     204   30    235   45    21    37   
 9 2     7     30    79    45    16    37   
10 1     118   30    91    45    18    37   
# ℹ 48 more rows


The repeated AGEP and JWMNP columns are gone, state is kept, and every column is consistently a character vector.
